courses.summary: Communicate clearly at work: business communication basics, active listening and presenting to a group.

lessons.title: Communication at work
lessons.why: Clear communication is valued in every job, and it matters more as AI handles routine tasks and people handle the conversations.
lessons.try: Rewrite a long email you sent recently so the main request is in the first sentence.

lessons.title: Active listening
lessons.why: Listening carefully prevents costly misunderstandings with colleagues and customers, and builds trust.
lessons.try: In your next conversation, summarise what the other person said before you reply, and ask if you got it right.

lessons.title: Public speaking
lessons.why: Presenting ideas confidently helps you lead meetings, train others and win support for your work.
lessons.try: Prepare a two-minute talk on a topic you know, with one slide, and practise it out loud.

quiz.q: Business communication takes place…
options: internally between employees and externally with other businesses and consumers
quiz.explain: It happens internally and externally, verbally and non-verbally.

quiz.q: What can stop a receiver from understanding a message?
quiz.explain: Barriers can prevent the receiver from understanding the sender.

quiz.q: The goal of active listening is to…
options: eliminate misunderstandings and establish clear communication
quiz.explain: Active listening aims to remove misunderstandings between speaker and listener.

quiz.q: Research shows that active listening…
quiz.explain: The lesson cites research showing it promotes trust.

quiz.q: Which three types of speech did Aristotle identify?
quiz.explain: Political, judicial and ceremonial speeches: deliberative, forensic and epideictic.

courses.summary: Deliver great service in the AI era: customer service basics, customer experience and working with chatbots.

lessons.title: Customer service
lessons.why: As AI handles routine questions, people in service roles focus on complex and emotional cases — skills that keep their value.
lessons.try: Write down the three customer questions you answer most often and the one that needs the most human judgement.

lessons.title: Customer experience
lessons.why: Customer experience covers every stage of contact, so improving one step can change how customers feel about the whole organisation.
lessons.try: Map the steps a customer goes through with your organisation, from first contact to after the purchase.

lessons.title: Chatbots
lessons.why: Chatbots now answer many routine questions, so knowing how they work helps you design good hand-offs to people.
lessons.try: Use a company's website chatbot and note the moment it should have handed you over to a person.

quiz.q: Good-quality customer service is usually measured through…
quiz.explain: The lesson says service quality is usually measured through customer retention.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, how are generative AI and automation changing customer contact work?
options: They resolve routine inquiries, so people focus on complex, emotionally nuanced cases
quiz.explain: Routine tier-1 work shrinks while human work concentrates on complex and escalated cases.

quiz.q: Customer experience (CX) covers…
options: all stages of interaction: before, during and after purchase
quiz.explain: CX includes pre-purchase, consumption and post-purchase.

quiz.q: A chatbot is…
options: software designed to converse through text or speech
quiz.explain: A chatbot functions as a conversation partner through text or speech.

quiz.q: Modern generative AI chatbots typically use…
quiz.explain: GenAI chatbots use fine-tuned LLMs to generate text.

courses.summary: Deliver work on time and on budget: project management basics, Scrum and Kanban boards.

lessons.title: Project management
lessons.why: Every change project — new systems, AI tools, process improvements — needs someone to keep scope, time and budget on track.
lessons.try: For a small project you know, write its scope, deadline and budget in one sentence each.

lessons.title: Scrum
lessons.why: Scrum is widely used in tech and beyond. Knowing sprints, stand-ups and retrospectives helps you join agile teams.
lessons.try: Plan a two-week sprint for a small goal: list the tasks and how you would review them at the end.

lessons.title: Kanban boards
lessons.why: A Kanban board makes work visible, so bottlenecks stand out and the team avoids taking on too much.
lessons.try: Set up a three-column board — To do, Doing, Done — for your tasks this week.

quiz.q: What are the primary constraints in project management?
quiz.explain: Scope, time and budget are the primary constraints.

quiz.q: In Scrum, work is completed within time-boxed iterations called…
quiz.explain: Sprints last no longer than a month and commonly two weeks.

quiz.q: How long can a daily scrum last at most?
quiz.explain: Daily scrums are time-boxed stand-ups of up to 15 minutes.

quiz.q: Which meeting at the end of a sprint is the team's internal reflection?
quiz.explain: The sprint review is for stakeholders; the retrospective is internal.

quiz.q: On a Kanban board, cards represent…
options: work items, moved across columns as they progress
quiz.explain: Cards are work items; columns are the stages of the process.

courses.summary: Lead people well: what leadership is, how coaching develops others, and why emotional intelligence matters.

lessons.title: Leadership
lessons.why: Leadership exists at every level, not only in management titles, and it grows in value as teams adapt to AI.
lessons.try: Recall a time you influenced a group decision without being the boss. What did you do?

lessons.title: Coaching
lessons.why: Coaching helps colleagues reach specific goals — a key part of helping a team learn new tools and ways of working.
lessons.try: Agree one specific goal with a colleague who is learning something new, and plan a short weekly check-in.

lessons.title: Emotional intelligence
lessons.why: Recognising and managing emotions — your own and other people's — helps you handle pressure, conflict and change.
lessons.try: After a difficult conversation, write down what you felt, what the other person probably felt, and what you would do differently.

quiz.q: Leadership is the ability to…
options: influence or guide other individuals, teams or organisations
quiz.explain: Leadership is about influencing or guiding others.

quiz.q: Some researchers argue that leadership is found…
options: at all levels of institutions, in formal and informal roles
quiz.explain: They challenge the view that leadership belongs to one person's role or authority.

quiz.q: Coaching differs from mentoring by focusing on…
quiz.explain: Mentoring covers broader development; coaching targets specific goals.

quiz.q: Emotional intelligence is the ability to…
options: perceive, use, understand, manage and handle emotions
quiz.explain: EI covers recognising and managing emotions in yourself and others.

quiz.q: Which 1995 bestseller popularised emotional intelligence?
quiz.explain: Daniel Goleman's 1995 book made the term popular.

courses.summary: Think clearly about problems: critical thinking, root cause analysis and the five whys.

lessons.title: Critical thinking
lessons.why: Analytical thinking is one of the skills employers value most, and checking AI outputs makes it even more important.
lessons.try: Take one claim from a recent news story or report and list the evidence for and against it.

lessons.title: Root cause analysis
lessons.why: Fixing the root cause stops a problem from coming back, instead of patching symptoms again and again.
lessons.try: Pick a recurring problem at work and write a timeline from normal operation to the moment it occurred.

lessons.title: The five whys
lessons.why: The five whys is a quick, low-cost way to dig below the obvious answer in a team discussion.
lessons.try: Run the five whys on a small problem, such as "the report was late", and write down each answer.

quiz.q: Critical thinking is the process of…
options: accepting the first answer you hear
analysing facts, evidence and arguments to reach sound conclusions
quiz.explain: It analyses facts and arguments to reach sound conclusions or informed choices.

quiz.q: According to Richard W. Paul, critical thinking…
quiz.explain: He argued critical thinking and analysis are competencies that can be learned.

quiz.q: Root cause analysis is used to…
options: identify the root causes of faults or problems
quiz.explain: RCA identifies root causes so that corrective actions prevent recurrence.

quiz.q: Which technique does ISO/IEC 31010 list for root cause analysis?
quiz.explain: Five whys, FMEA, fault tree analysis, Ishikawa diagrams and Pareto analysis are listed.

quiz.q: Who described the five whys technique?
quiz.explain: Taiichi Ohno described it at Toyota Motor Corporation.

courses.summary: Generate and shape new ideas: design thinking, brainstorming and lateral thinking.

lessons.title: Design thinking
lessons.why: Creative thinking is rising in importance as AI takes over routine work, and design thinking gives it a practical process.
lessons.try: Interview one customer or colleague about a frustration, then write three ideas to solve it.

lessons.title: Brainstorming
lessons.why: Brainstorming gets many ideas on the table fast — and the best idea is often not the first one.
lessons.try: Set a 10-minute timer and list as many ideas as you can for one problem, without judging any of them.

lessons.title: Lateral thinking
lessons.why: Lateral thinking helps you escape the obvious solution, which is useful when the usual approach keeps failing.
lessons.try: Take a problem and ask: what would we do if the usual solution were not allowed?

quiz.q: Design thinking refers to…
options: the cognitive, strategic and practical procedures designers use
quiz.explain: It is the set of procedures designers use, applied to innovation in products and services.

quiz.q: During brainstorming, ideas are…
options: noted down but not judged until later
quiz.explain: Criticism is held back so people are not inhibited.

quiz.q: Who popularised the term brainstorming?
quiz.explain: Alex Osborn popularised it in Applied Imagination (1953).

quiz.q: Lateral thinking means…
options: solving problems with an indirect, creative approach that is not immediately obvious
quiz.explain: It is often described as thinking outside the box.

quiz.q: Who first used the term lateral thinking, in 1967?
quiz.explain: The Maltese psychologist Edward de Bono coined the term.

courses.summary: Help others learn: instructional design, how adults learn, and the ADDIE model for building training.

lessons.title: Instructional design
lessons.why: Every organisation adopting AI needs people who can teach colleagues new tools — a growing role for experienced staff.
lessons.try: Write one clear learning goal for a short training session you could give at work.

lessons.title: How adults learn
lessons.why: Adults learn best when learning meets their needs and they take responsibility for it, so design your training around that.
lessons.try: Ask two colleagues what they most need to learn this year and how they prefer to learn.

lessons.title: The ADDIE model
lessons.why: ADDIE gives you a simple checklist so training is planned, built, delivered and then improved.
lessons.try: Write one sentence for each ADDIE phase for a 30-minute session on a tool you use.

quiz.q: Instructional design is the practice of…
options: systematically designing, developing and delivering instructional materials and experiences
quiz.explain: ID designs learning experiences in a consistent, reliable way.

quiz.q: The instructional design process begins by…
options: determining the state and needs of the learner
quiz.explain: First understand the learner, then define the goal and the intervention.

quiz.q: Which kind of adult learning is organised by institutions but carries no credential?
quiz.explain: Non-formal learning is organised but non-credential, often in the workplace.

quiz.q: What do the letters ADDIE stand for?
quiz.explain: ADDIE names its five phases.

quiz.q: Which is mentioned as a common alternative to ADDIE?
quiz.explain: Rapid prototyping is another common alternative.

courses.summary: Keep accurate books: bookkeeping basics, double-entry and reconciliation.

lessons.title: Bookkeeping
lessons.why: Bookkeeping is changing fast as AI reads invoices automatically. Knowing the principles helps you move into checking, analysis and advisory work.
lessons.try: List the source documents your team handles in a month: invoices, receipts, payment slips.

lessons.title: Double-entry bookkeeping
lessons.why: Double-entry keeps the books balanced, which makes errors and fraud easier to detect.
lessons.try: Record a cash purchase of equipment as two entries: one asset goes up and another goes down.

lessons.title: Bank reconciliation
lessons.why: Reconciliation catches missing payments, duplicates and fraud before they become expensive problems.
lessons.try: Compare one week of bank statement lines with your records and mark any that do not match.

quiz.q: Bookkeeping is…
quiz.explain: Bookkeeping records financial transactions as part of accounting.

quiz.q: Who usually prepares financial reports from the bookkeeper's records?
quiz.explain: The bookkeeper reaches the trial balance; the accountant prepares the reports.

quiz.q: In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction is recorded with…
options: equal and opposite entries (debits and credits)
quiz.explain: Equal and opposite entries keep the books balanced.

quiz.q: What is the accounting equation?
quiz.explain: Every transaction keeps Assets = Liabilities + Equity in balance.

quiz.q: Reconciliation ensures that…
options: two sets of records are in agreement
quiz.explain: It checks that two sets of records, usually account balances, match.

courses.summary: Move beyond keying in data: what data entry involves, how validation protects quality, and how OCR is changing the job.

lessons.title: Data entry work
lessons.why: Data entry is among the fastest-declining jobs, so knowing where it is heading helps you plan your next step.
lessons.try: Time yourself entering ten records and note which errors happen most often.

lessons.title: Data validation
lessons.why: Validation rules stop bad data at the door. Designing and checking them is a step up from typing data in.
lessons.try: Write three validation rules for a customer form, for example: a date of birth cannot be in the future.

lessons.title: Optical character recognition
lessons.why: OCR and AI now read invoices and forms automatically. People who can check, correct and improve these systems stay in demand.
lessons.try: Photograph a printed document, run it through a free OCR app, and count the errors in the extracted text.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what are the key measures of a data entry clerk's job?
quiz.explain: Speed and accuracy are the key measures.

quiz.q: Data is often entered into a computer from…
quiz.explain: Clerks often key in data from paper documents.

quiz.q: Data validation checks input data for…
quiz.explain: Validation rules check correctness, meaningfulness and security.

quiz.q: Optical character recognition (OCR) converts…
options: images of typed, handwritten or printed text into machine-encoded text
quiz.explain: OCR digitises text from scans and photos.

quiz.q: How did early OCR systems differ from modern ones?
options: They had to be trained on each character and worked on one font at a time
quiz.explain: Modern systems handle most fonts with high accuracy.

courses.summary: Create clear visual communication: graphic design, typography and colour theory.

lessons.title: Graphic design
lessons.why: AI can now generate images quickly, so a designer's lasting value lies in understanding the message, the audience and the brand.
lessons.try: Pick a poster or social media post you like and write down the single message it communicates.

lessons.title: Typography
lessons.why: Good typography makes text easy to read — a skill that matters in reports, slides and websites, not only in design studios.
lessons.try: Reformat one slide using a single typeface, two sizes and more space between lines, and compare it with the original.

lessons.title: Colour theory
lessons.why: Colour choices affect readability, mood and accessibility, so understanding harmony and contrast improves any design.
lessons.try: Check the contrast between the text and background colours of one of your designs with a free online contrast checker.

quiz.q: Graphic design creates visual communications intended to…
options: transmit specific messages to social groups
quiz.explain: It communicates specific messages with specific objectives.

quiz.q: In the communication process, the graphic designer acts as…
options: the encoder or interpreter of the message
quiz.explain: Designers interpret, order and present visual messages.

quiz.q: Typography is the art and technique of…
options: arranging type to make written language legible and readable
quiz.explain: Typography arranges type for legibility and readability.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of arranging type?
options: Selecting typefaces, point sizes and line spacing
quiz.explain: Typefaces, sizes, line lengths and spacing are all typographic choices.

quiz.q: Colour theory describes…
options: colour mixing, contrast effects, harmony and symbolism
quiz.explain: It is a body of knowledge about how colours behave together.

courses.summary: Understand how health care works, how electronic health records are used, and why patient safety matters.

lessons.title: Health care
lessons.why: Health care is a large employer, and technology roles in health need people who understand how care is delivered.
lessons.try: List the health services your family used last year: primary care, hospital, pharmacy, dental.

lessons.title: Electronic health records
lessons.why: EHRs bring patient data together, making them the foundation of health analytics and digital health jobs.
lessons.try: List five types of information an electronic health record contains, and who should be allowed to see each.

lessons.title: Patient safety
lessons.why: Preventing harm is everyone's job in health care, including the people who build and run its digital systems.
lessons.try: Think of a hand-over between two people at work or in a clinic, and list what information could get lost.

quiz.q: Health care improves or maintains health through…
options: prevention, diagnosis, treatment and cure of illness and injury
quiz.explain: Health care spans prevention, diagnosis, treatment and cure.

quiz.q: Which barrier to health care access is mentioned in the lesson?
options: Financial limitations such as insurance coverage
quiz.explain: Financial, geographical, sociocultural and personal limitations affect access.

quiz.q: An electronic health record (EHR) is…
options: a systematised digital collection of patient and population health information
quiz.explain: EHRs store health information digitally and can be shared across settings.

quiz.q: Patient safety focuses on…
options: preventing, reducing, reporting and analysing medical errors and preventable harm
quiz.explain: Patient safety systematically prevents and analyses medical errors.

quiz.q: According to the WHO figure in the lesson, how many patients globally experience harm due to health care errors?
quiz.explain: The WHO identified that 1 in 10 patients experience harm.

courses.summary: Keep learning for life: why it matters, how spaced repetition helps memory, and how to think about your own thinking.

lessons.title: Lifelong learning
lessons.why: Skills change faster than careers, so steady learning keeps you employable as AI reshapes jobs.
lessons.try: Set one learning goal for the next month and block a regular time slot for it in your calendar.

lessons.title: Spaced repetition
lessons.why: Reviewing material at increasing intervals helps you remember far more with the same study time.
lessons.try: Make five flashcards about something you are learning and review them tomorrow, in three days and next week.

lessons.title: Thinking about your thinking
lessons.why: Knowing how you learn best helps you choose strategies that work and notice when you are stuck.
lessons.try: After your next study session, write down what worked, what didn't, and one change you will try.

quiz.q: Lifelong learning is…
options: the ongoing, voluntary and self-motivated pursuit of learning
quiz.explain: It is ongoing, voluntary and self-motivated.

quiz.q: Why is lifelong learning important, according to the lesson?
options: It replaces the need for work
It is required by every employer
quiz.explain: It also enhances social inclusion, active citizenship and personal development.

quiz.q: In spaced repetition, difficult flashcards are shown…
quiz.explain: New and difficult cards appear more often; easy ones less often.

quiz.q: Spaced repetition exploits which psychological effect?
quiz.explain: It uses the spacing effect to improve memory.

quiz.q: Metacognition means…
quiz.explain: It is awareness and understanding of your own thought processes.

courses.summary: Read the numbers behind a business: financial analysis, budgets and financial statements.

lessons.title: Financial analysis
lessons.why: Financial analysis turns reports into decisions — buy or lease, borrow or not — and pairs well with data and AI skills.
lessons.try: Look at a company's published annual report and find its revenue and profit for the last two years.

lessons.title: Budgets
lessons.why: Budgets turn plans into numbers, so you can set priorities and check progress during the year.
lessons.try: Make a simple monthly budget for a team activity with expected income and costs, and check whether it ends in surplus or deficit.

lessons.title: Financial statements
lessons.why: Financial statements are the common language of business. Reading them lets you judge an organisation's health.
lessons.try: Find a published balance sheet and check that assets equal liabilities plus equity.

quiz.q: Financial analysis assesses a business's…
quiz.explain: It assesses viability, stability and profitability.

quiz.q: Which decision can financial analysis support?
options: Whether to buy or lease machinery
quiz.explain: It informs decisions such as acquiring or leasing equipment.

quiz.q: When expenses exceed income, a budget shows a…
quiz.explain: A deficit means expenses exceed income; a surplus is the opposite.

quiz.q: A balance sheet reports…
options: assets, liabilities and owners' equity at a point in time
quiz.explain: A balance sheet is a snapshot at a point in time.

quiz.q: Which statement reports income, expenses and profits over a period?
quiz.explain: The income statement covers an accounting period.
